name: Kiliwa
confidence_why: Kiliwa's root-based stress with a lexical pitch accent rests on one fieldworker, Mixco (1983, 1985, 1996, 2000), whose concordant descriptions are endorsed by the Yuman surveys of Langdon 1977 and Miller 2023, and the only dissent is on detail (Langdon 1977 counts two functional pitches to Mixco's three; Mixco's own 'generally penultimate' headline sits beside his root-final rule) or comes from a question-marked second-hand entry in Hyman 1977's typology tables.

catalog_quote: Pitch Accent Given that stress in Kiliwa is a composite of pitch and ... Long syllables have a long vowel written as a geminate vowel. Phonemic pitch accent is restricted, generally speaking, to the penultimate syllable. Exceptions are dealt with in what follows. Note that pitch accent plays a minimally distinctive role in the language. There are three phonemics accents: (1) high ... Pitch Accent Minimal Pairs: (1) high: ?-saa (1) 'yucca cactus fruit' [?sáá] (2) falling: ?-saa (2) 'juniper' [?saa] (3) low: ?-sii (3) 'buzzard; vulture' [?ósèè] Turning to the few exceptions having a non-penultimate stress pattern, these are predictable in a two-part rule: the accent will be final in a multisyllabic root ending in a long vowel or a consonant; otherwise stress is penultimate. Moreover, there are a set of trisyllabic roots (all included here); there are also some disyllabic roots ending in a final /i/ or /u/. The trisyllabic roots are: xiwalu 'sotol (plant) ... The majority of disyllabic roots follow the aforementioned rule: -ihaa 'to go', -ihaas 'lightweight', -ima? 'to/a dance', -uhaa 'to arrive', -umaay 'man's son', -uñaay 'take along', wñiiy 'want; desire', xi ... [Mixco 1985] As in other Yuman languages, Kiliwa stress is predictable for the vast majority of roots. Stress in Kiliwa is a composite phenomenon consisting of loudness and an unpredictable level of pitch; stress can thus be referred to as pitch accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (realised as loudness plus a lexically unpredictable pitch: high, falling or low -- hence 'pitch accent') sits on the morphological root; prefixes and suffixes are unstressed. Most roots are monosyllabic, so the root vowel carries the accent; in the minority of polysyllabic roots the accent is penultimate (Mixco 1983: 'the first root syllable is predictably louder than the others; roots rarely exceed two syllables') unless the root ends in a long vowel or a consonant, in which case it is root-final (Mixco 2000). Mixco 1985 adds: 'As in other Yuman languages, Kiliwa stress is predictable for the vast majority of roots.. stress can thus be referred to as pitch accent.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: A closed set of trisyllabic roots (xiwalu 'sotol', xiwilu..) and some disyllabic roots ending in short /i/ or /u/ are listed as special cases; polysyllabic roots are said to result from accretion of old prefixal material (čxpaa 'to straddle').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root within the word (root marked with '+' in Mixco's transcriptions so the stress rule can be applied); pitch level on the stressed vowel is lexical (three-way contrast, falling only on long vowels) and 'plays no major grammatical role' (Mixco 1983). Statement assembled from Google Books snippets of three Mixco works; full pages not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Kiliwa proper (kili1268; Mixco's fieldwork at Arroyo León, Baja California, principal consultant Rufino Ochurte); no dialect split is reported. The family-level statements (Langdon 1977, Wares 1968, Miller 2023) are about Yuman generally, not Kiliwa specifically.

new_statements.quote: Dado que el acento en kiliwa es un complejo de tono y de intensidad, se le debe denominar acento tónico. [...] El acento es, por lo general, predecible en la sílaba penúltima. Las excepciones se aclaran en lo que sigue. Nótese que las diferencias tónicas juegan un papel mínimo en la estructura [...] En torno a los raros ejemplos de acentuación no-penúltima afirmaríamos que se puede predecir por medio de una regla en dos partes: caerá el acento en la sílaba final de una raíz multisilábica que termine en consonante o en vocal larga; de otra manera, el acento será penúltimo.[34] Hay además una cuantas raíces trisilábicas (incluidas aquí) y otras cuantas disilábicas con una /i/ o una /u/ final.
new_statements.translation: Since accent in Kiliwa is a composite of pitch and intensity, it should be called pitch accent (acento tónico). [...] The accent is, in general, predictable on the penultimate syllable. The exceptions are clarified in what follows. Note that the pitch differences play a minimal role in the structure [...] As for the rare examples of non-penultimate accentuation, we would hold that it can be predicted by a two-part rule: the accent will fall on the final syllable of a multisyllabic root ending in a consonant or a long vowel; otherwise the accent will be penultimate.[34] There are in addition a few trisyllabic roots (included here) and a few other disyllabic ones with a final /i/ or /u/.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the Spanish version of the very passage already in existing_statements from Mixco 2000 (LINCOM): same three pitches, same 'generally penultimate' headline, same two-part rule (final in a multisyllabic root ending in C or long V, otherwise penultimate), same lists of exceptional roots. It confirms the catalog's 'morphologically determined' record and supplies the Spanish wording; it adds nothing the 2000 sketch does not already say.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress ('acento tónico', a composite of pitch and intensity, with three lexical pitches carrying minimal functional load) is predictable and sits on the root. Within a multisyllabic root it is weight-sensitive: on the final syllable if the root ends in a consonant or a long vowel, otherwise on the penultimate; the author's headline formulation is 'generally penultimate', with a closed list of trisyllabic roots (xiwalu, xiwilu, ti?payu, sk(u)wanu) and disyllabic roots in final short /i/ or /u/ as the penultimate cases, while 'the majority of disyllabic roots' follow the final-heavy-syllable clause (-ihaa, -ihaas..).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets obtained.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic roots xiwalu 'sotol', xiwilu 'planta', ti?payu 'águila', sk(u)wanu 'la sien' and disyllabic roots ending in short /i/ or /u/ (Caqi 'caer', -Caxu 'aburrido', -ma?i 'cielo', -x?ilu 'liebre') take penultimate accent; other disyllabic roots ending in a consonant or long vowel take final accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Mixco 1996 describes the Kiliwa of Arroyo León, Baja California (Mixco's own consultants; the editors' Introducción refers to his Kiliwa Texts). Langdon 1977's Kiliwa data are entirely from Mixco 1971 (UC Berkeley dissertation) and his unpublished field notes (fn. 8, p. 257), so the two works describe the same variety.

new_statements.quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. [...] Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes. [p. 239] Note that regardless of the complexity of the word, the stress remains fixed on the root. [p. 240] For Kiliwa, Mixco (1971) claims not only the 3 vowel qualities, each occurring both short and long, but also contrastive pitches, three for long vowels (high, low, and high-falling), two for short vowels (high and low). [p. 242] it is probable that no more than two contrastive pitches are truly functional in Kiliwa. [p. 243]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's morphologically-determined (root) reading and with Mixco's 'pitch accent' characterisation, and adds: the domain statement (stress fixed on the root; word-final tendency from prefixing), secondary stress in compounds, the loss of unstressed length in Kiliwa, and an independent count of the pitch contrasts (3 long / 2 short, probably only 2 functional) that is slightly leaner than Mixco 1996/2000's three phonemic pitches. Says nothing about the within-root two-part rule. All Kiliwa data come from Mixco 1971 and his field notes (fn. 8).
new_statements.rule_in_words: For every Yuman language including Kiliwa (listed in the classification on p. 239), stress is assigned morphologically to the root, which is canonically a monosyllable; because derivational affixes are overwhelmingly prefixes, uninflected words tend to come out with final stress, but the stress stays fixed on the root however complex the word. 'Stress' is a bundle of loudness, pitch and length. Kiliwa-specific content is about pitch: three contrastive pitches on long vowels and two on short (after Mixco 1971), of which probably only two are functional; unstressed vowels take high pitch before glottal stop and otherwise the inverse of the stressed syllable's pitch (pp. 243-244); Kiliwa has lost length contrasts in unstressed position (p. 240).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 240: 'The only thing that can happen to a stressed syllable is that the stress reduces in compound formation to secondary stress on the first member of the compound, thus maintaining the preference for primary stress on the last syllable' (stated for Yuman generally, illustrated with Diegueño compounds; may reduce further to unstressed).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kiliwa placement; fluctuation of pitch across forms of the same root (p. 243, ex. 11). Mojave is singled out as the only Yuman language with stress shifts (p. 240).
new_statements.identity_note: Mixco 1996 describes the Kiliwa of Arroyo León, Baja California (Mixco's own consultants; the editors' Introducción refers to his Kiliwa Texts). Langdon 1977's Kiliwa data are entirely from Mixco 1971 (UC Berkeley dissertation) and his unpublished field notes (fn. 8, p. 257), so the two works describe the same variety.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on the core fact that Kiliwa stress sits on the root and carries a lexical pitch. Differences are of formulation and domain: Mixco 1996 (and 2000) headline 'por lo general.. penúltima' while his own two-part rule makes the majority of disyllabic roots root-final (as Mixco 1985 puts it, 'preponderantly on the last long or closed syllable'), and Langdon 1977 says uninflected Yuman words 'tend to have stress on the last syllable'; these are statements about roots vs. words and about which case is called the default, not different placements. Langdon (p. 243) thinks only two Kiliwa pitches are functional against Mixco's three phonemic pitches (falling restricted to long vowels) -- an inventory disagreement, not a placement one. In the same SCOPIL 4 volume, Hyman's typology tables list 'Kiliwa? (tone)' under dominant initial stress (p. 60) and 'Kiliwa (R)' [source Ruhlen 1975] under dominant final stress (p. 65); this internal inconsistency of a secondary survey should not be taken as a primary claim about Kiliwa.
